name: Graphite Grey
lede: Graphite Grey is a dark, slightly blue-tinged grey named for the soft carbon of pencils, a mineral that contains no lead.

sections.title: The mineral
sections.body: Paterson defines graphite as a dark metallic grey, also called graphite grey, made from crystallised carbon [1]. A flat swatch cannot show that sheen, which in life is part of the color [1][2].

sections.title: Pencil lead without lead
sections.body:
Pencil lead contains no lead. Since the mid-sixteenth century it has been graphite, first found at Borrowdale in England's Lake District, with a legend dating the find to 1565 [3]. Before that European artists drew in silverpoint, and Cortés recorded in 1519 that the Aztecs used crayons of a grey mineral [3].

Borrowdale graphite was so valuable that the mine opened only about seven weeks a year, workers were searched, and an act of 1752 threatened smugglers [3]. In 1794 Nicolas Conté showed that low-grade French graphite, powdered and mixed with clay, would make pencils; more clay gives a harder pencil and less a softer, blacker one [3].

sections.title: Swatch and shine
sections.body: Finlay describes the hair shirt of St Thomas More at Buckfast Abbey as a slippery silvery grey like graphite that shines in the light [2]. Our library carries the color in Ridgway's standards of 1912, a RAL list of 1927 and the ISCC-NBS of 1955, nearest to dark bluish gray by 4.5 units of ΔE2000 [4]. See also [[charcoal-grey]], [[gunmetal]] and [[payne-s-grey]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This tone appears in 273 paintings in our archive, 1.15 per cent, as photographed [5]. Norway stands out, with it in 9 of 120 paintings [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [5].
